label: Corning ADSS 12F aerial, G.652.D
notes: Corning 012ELE-T3322A20 product spec sheet (Corning Optical Communications ecatalog, revision date 2026-11-28): 'Aerial Dielectric Self-Supporting Cable, ADSS 12 F, Single-mode (OS2), A-D2Y(T)2Y, (1 x 12)'. Construction A-D2Y(T)2Y per EN 60794-1-1 (DIN VDE 0888-100-1): one active loose tube of 12 fibres in twelve tube positions with eleven filling elements, dielectric central element, a DRY core held by swellable elements rather than gel, non-metallic (aramid) strength members over the core, black PE jacket, halogen-free; 15.1 mm nominal diameter, 161 kg/km, crush 3000 N/10 cm, max tensile 1700 N long-term / 4000 N short-term, min bend radius 265 mm installation / 225 mm operation, -40 to +70 C operating and storage (-5 to +50 C installation), Telcordia colour code, ITU-T G.652.D / IEC 60793-2-50 B1.3 fibre, cable cutoff 1260 nm, PMD link design value <= 0.06 ps/sqrt(km). Why the row exists: every feeder cable in this catalogue until now is gel-filled loose tube for duct or direct burial - a cable that needs a duct, a trench or a tray, and whose published data says nothing about carrying its own weight between poles. An aerial FTTH plant (pole route, lashed or on strand) had no cable to name, so the BOM bought duct cable for a pole line. This is the catalogue's first aerial row, and the 12F size is the one a spur or a single-pole extension uses. Attenuation, and exactly what kind of figure it is: the sheet publishes MAXIMUM 0.36 dB/km at 1310 nm, 0.36 at 1383 nm and 0.22 at 1550 nm - maxima, not typicals, and no 1490 nm figure at all. This row carries 0.35 / 0.22 / 0.21, the same typical installed row g652d-loose-12, g657a2-drop-2 and g657a2-indoor-12 carry, deliberately: budgeting one aerial span at a factory maximum while its duct neighbours are budgeted at typicals prices the same design two different ways. 1490 nm is interpolated between the two published windows and is not a citation from Corning or from ITU-T. Corning's 0.36 dB/km at 1310 nm sits 0.01 dB/km above the 0.35 here, so hold the supplier to 0.36 in the acceptance test and read the as-built OTDR for a budget that gets signed. The row publishes NO drumM, and that is a decision: Corning's Dimensions block prints 'Max. cable length per reel/drum 6000 m', which is a ceiling and not a putup list, and declaring it would make the BOM buy a 6 km reel for a short aerial spur - measured on engine/length.js at 0.7 km of route a 6000 m drum bills 6,000 m where a 2,000 m drum bills 2,000, and at 12 km it bills 18,000 m against 14,000; only between 4.8 and 6 km do the two agree. With no drumM the engine falls back to engine/length.js default of 2,000 m, and the BOM row carries 2,000 m and no field saying whether that is a drum or the engine default - measured on an eight-house estate (706.3 m of design length) the row comes back drumM 2000, one drum, 2,000 m purchased, 1,293.73 m spare - so enter the reel actually ordered. What the engine does not model, and one trap: CABLE_USES has no 'aerial' value, so aerial-ness lives in the tags and this note and nothing in the planner reads it; nothing checks span, sag, ice or wind loading, so the design will run this cable over any span you draw and the pole-to-pole distance stays a decision the planner takes; nothing metallic means nothing to bond or earth at a joint, which is a fact rather than a field. The trap is the tie-break: cableFor answers with the SMALLEST cable that fits and breaks ties on model id, and 'g652d-adss-12' sorts before 'g652d-loose-12', so a ladder naming both buys aerial cable for every 12-fibre span in the plant - name this row instead of its duct twin, not beside it. This row also deliberately does not say 'drop': isDropCable in engine/design.js reads `use` to REFUSE a span that ended up on drop cable beyond 300 m or bundled, and a 2-fibre aerial spur is still an ADSS span, not tight-buffer G.657.A2 flat drop. One product data sheet's figures, not a measured build: replace with the cable actually purchased and its as-built attenuation before ordering.
